title: A warrior living on air
hook: Arjuna fasts until he lives on air, the sages feel the heat of his tapas, and Shiva says he already knows Arjuna's heart
carry: tapas: discipline offered to God, not shown
tomorrow: who is the hunter with the bow?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities began with a test. Indra, in disguise, told him to throw away his bow, and he kept to his own path. Your line was svadharma: walk your own path, not another's.

A warrior in grass clothes. That's what the sages on the mountain see when they look at the newcomer. Arjuna, prince and archer, has traded his royal dress for rags of grass and a deerskin, and taken up a staff. He's come to the foot of the Himalayas to do one thing: draw the attention of Shiva. And the way he sets about it is tapas, the slow, burning work of austerity.
screen: `A WARRIOR IN GRASS CLOTHES.` → `TO DRAW SHIVA'S ATTENTION.` → `THE BURNING WORK OF TAPAS.`

segments.voice: The epic describes it step by step. At first Arjuna eats fruit, but only every few nights. Then less often. Month by month he narrows his life, until he lives on air alone, standing on the tips of his toes with his arms raised. In this story, tapas burns, and the burning is real. The sages who live on the mountain feel it; smoke, in the epic's telling, seems to rise from the earth around him. Worried, they go to Shiva: who is this man, and what is he doing? Shiva's answer is calm. Don't worry. I know what's in Arjuna's heart. I know what he wants. Go back, and be at peace. Arjuna hasn't said a word to Shiva. His discipline has spoken for him. That's tapas, one of Hinduism's oldest ideas: discipline as a fire, offered to God. It's why Hindu homes still keep vratas, vows of fasting and restraint. Many keep Mondays for Shiva, fasting or eating simply until evening. Many fast on Ekadashi for Vishnu, or stay awake through the night of Maha Shivaratri. The point isn't to suffer, and it isn't to be seen. Shiva knew Arjuna's heart before Arjuna said a word. In a vrat, the fast is how the heart speaks back.
screen: `LESS FOOD, THEN ONLY AIR.` · `TAPAS GIVES OFF HEAT.` · `SHIVA ALREADY KNOWS.` · then, large: `TAPAS: DISCIPLINE OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Hindus who keep a vrat often begin with a sankalpa, a quiet intention. Try a small one now: choose one thing to go without today, a snack, a scroll, a complaint. Breathe in and name it; breathe out and offer it, to Shiva or to God as you know God. If you don't pray, offer it for someone you love. Then keep it quietly; no one else needs to know.
Arjuna's austerities. Less food, then only air, a heat the sages felt, and a god who already knew his heart.
Your line: tapas: discipline offered to God, not shown. Shiva heard Arjuna's without a single word. Tomorrow: who is the hunter with the bow? Day seven hundred eighty-three, done.
